```suggestion
			if ((member_drop_modifier_pressed || export_drop_modifier_pressed) && ResourceLoader::exists(path)) {
```
Cheaper condition first.

`p_dragged_export_refs` is only iterated over and it is not used like a dictionary, so it shouldn't be one. Also being a signal bind limits it, so it can just be a class variable.
It can be a `LocalVector<DraggedExport>` where `DraggedExport` is a new struct with two variables, the variable name and the variant.

I think this needs to use the undo redo system to handle setting it, and treat it as a separate action from dropping the text. Or at least mark the scene as dirty, otherwise the user could close it without saving.

```suggestion
	// Assign dragged exported variables after script changes.
```
Use sentence case for all comments.

There doesn't need to be a warning popup when there is no scene. It should act the same way as when a different scene is selected, where it still makes the exported variable but doesn't assign it.
Same with the one below.

This would be useful for Resource types as well, we shouldn't prevent it for any Objects.
It's only Nodes and maybe Resources that can also be assigned afterwards.
For Resources, I think we can get the FileSystems selected paths, not sure.

This needs to only set on the script, in case the variable name is the same as another one, we only want it to set on the instance.
For example, make a script called `script.gd` and try to drop it, it will replace the script on the node without an undo option.
I think we can use `sn->get_script_instance()` and set it on that instead.


We can also try to improve the variable name generation to avoid conflicts, but it should probably be in a separate PR.

`edited_script_changed` isn't the right place for this. If you set the Script completion idle parse delay very high (in editor settings) and then save, you can see that the exported variable will appear in the inspector, but it won't be set until the idle parse happens.
I think `_assign_dragged_export_variables` needs to be called from `apply_code` and `_validate_script` instead.
Yeah, I thought improving the variable name generation as well, I might do it on a follow up PR.

for resources you should check (cpp equivalent to) `EditorInterface.get_inspector().get_edited_object()`

Alternatively you could try to get all files that has the script as dependency and see if they are resources inheriting it, but i dont think that is really desired, changing all the files in the filesystem could be or not what the user wants, and we should not try to guess that

How would it make sense specifically for resources? Since if you are drag n dropping onto a resource script, we would need an instance of the resource if we want to set it to something. And even then its only one resource instance. Not really sure how much it makes sense. I'm not opposed to still making creating the `@export` line, and just not assigning anything to it afterwards.

We would need to get the selected resource instance from the file system, like how we get the node instance from the current scene. Actually we might have to go through all of the resources to find them, since the user probably isn't going to be selecting them.
But that could be done later, for now it is fine to just create the `@export` line since it is still useful.

I think I would rather opt for the second option. I tried using undo redo, but it kind of makes undoing in the scene not undo anything if the you just undid the line in the script, or if the variable doesn't exist anymore all together.

Yeah, tested it and it seems you are right, it works better with any type of configuration I tried tackling it with.

One thing though is I had some bug where the editor crashed after changing the idle parse delay in between the export variables updating (changing from high to low). Couldn't recreate it though.

These can all be above in the private section, since they don't need to be protected. 
Though I am not sure why there is so many things in the protected section in the first place for this file...

asigning the value to every single instance existing is a bad idea, is very probablt not what the user wants to do, `EditorInterface.get_inspector().get_edited_object()` gives you the object that is being edited in the inspector, if that object happens to be a Resource, and that Resource happens to have assigned this script, then would make sense to assign the value, otherwise i would not want to assign a value to anything, because will cause in most of the cases the need of the user to go to the resources one by one to clear it
